en: And scatter his full fortune.
Declaring, ‘I am the khan’s son,’
I shall take the road to Chardak,
Test how much strength he has,
Learn how great his power is,
And enter into his vast wealth.
I shall rain shots upon him.
My sorrowful uncle Bakai,
My grandsire left by my father,
My khan whose back is like a mountain,
My elder, like a prophet,
He who wears a blue lynx cap,
The handsomest among all men,
My sacred old man,
My khan and uncle Bakai—
If I do not cross the hills to seek him
And set him free;
If I do not rescue old Bakai, my heirloom,
Whole and unharmed;
If I do not go to Khan Kanchoro
And unleash cold havoc upon the world
For what he will not yield when asked;
If he will not surrender the possessions through counsel,
If I do not seize them without another word!”
So the hero Seytek spoke,
Preparing himself in fury,
Raging like a lion.
His heart surged with many feelings,
And he looked like a lofty blue crag
As he stood before them.
Külchoro, sustained by the patron spirit,
Spoke slowly and firmly,
Beginning his counsel to brave Seytek:
“Ah, you are my beloved, my mainstay,
My lion left by the bloodthirsty hero.
You are the banner fixed upon my spear,
The support of this entrusted life,
A cherished gift cradled in song.
You are the joy before my eyes,
My child Seytek, my good fortune.
When I behold you, my belly is full;
Without you, my cherished one, I have no life.
I shall strike the swaggering, wrathful enemy
Across the nape of his neck;
Even if he has sixty lives,
I shall slaughter him and leave none!
I shall charge in and test
His courage and valor;
I shall divide all his wealth.
With that fiercely wrathful swine
I shall grapple without cease.
If Kanchoro, whom I fight,
Is a warrior and a hero,
A lion who has shaken the world,
Then, if fate decrees, let me die
And let my youthful head behold
The true realm from which none return.
How could I surrender my honor
To that strutting false kinsman?
Boastful Kanchoro,
If your death comes suddenly,
If disaster strikes by chance,
May my perfect mother Aichürök,
Saying, ‘My son died in battle,’
Forgive me through her grief.
For the milk of her white breast,
May my lion mother forgive me.
How could I endure alive
The humiliation he has inflicted?
If I do not repay shame with shame
And relentlessly take my vengeance,
May I sink away as though never born.
He boasts of valor and lionhood,
That consummate, depraved lecher,
Posing as righteous and heroic.
If I do not somehow settle accounts
With cunning Kanchoro,
Going tirelessly upon the road;
If I do not beat the circling madness
Out of that white-deviled swine,
May I die without human honor,
May I sink away as though never born.
Your uncle Külchoro is such a man:
Your support when you climb,
Your prop when you descend;
Your clear road across the hills,
Your countless army when he leads.
My gray fledgling falcon
Would not let a bustard escape the steppe.
I am black steel with a lamb-liver sheen,
Such as no smith could find.
I am your warrior, proven among heroes;
When I lead the first attack,
I am your keen-eyed Choro of old.
Not merely keen-eyed Külchoro—
I am one tested by many nations.
If you thrust me against a stubborn foe,
I am a sharp, steel-headed spear,
Aimed exactly where you intend.
If you unleash me upon the chosen foe,
I am a dark, double-edged blade.
I am Külchoro indeed,
The renowned lion and tiger
Who crushes the foe he faces.
Set the dawn as our appointed time
And take your uncle Kül as companion.
I shall teach you what you do not know,
And knowingly lead you against the foe.
I shall be a banner to your kin;
If you unleash me upon your enemy,
I shall be a singular black poison
That bursts lungs and spills gall.
While your tiger father lived,
He would wreak utter slaughter
Upon the Chinese encamped on the heights.
If I was left afoot in dangerous ground,
Your precious gray-maned lion of a father
Would take me up behind him.
He never said, ‘There is no room behind me,’
Nor, ‘Let this poor wretch
Stay safely behind to tend the horses.’
I possessed the strength for battle.
Your forefather was a gray-maned lion.
The baggage train and scouting,
The fighting and lionheartedness,
Every manner of heroic deed—
While my mighty uncle lived,
He would say, ‘Let my Külchoro learn.’
Parted from that mighty hero,
I became like a magpie without a tail,
Like a kulan caught in a snare.
I became like a man without feet,
Like a writhing snake.
Sobbing, lamenting, and grieving,
Parted from the bloodthirsty lion,
I was left like a lesser wife.
Parted from my soul’s companion,
I was left helpless.
Let us head upstream through broad Talas,
Land of rivers and springs.
Do not be headstrong, my Seytek;
Let the two of us go together.
Let us go and possess the land of Talas,
And lead the white-capped Kyrgyz people,
Raising an uproar before all who see,
Raising a clamor to the blue sky.
Let the two of us go together.
If you take the road alone,
You are not yet past thirteen;
The fierceness of your mother’s breast
Has not yet left your palate.
Your strength and vigor are not yet full;
The time has not yet come
For you to ride out alone.
Choose the hour of dawn for our meeting
And take your uncle Kül as companion.
If you take your uncle with you,
He will show you your grandsire Bakai.
If, my colt, you display your skill
And accomplish many heroic deeds,
When you reach the place where warriors clash,
Your servant-uncle will hold your horse.
You need a dark gray-maned lion
Who is never sated by countless armies
And spares no life when facing the foe.
When enemies meet you in battle,
You need a lion like me.
Set our meeting by the morning star
And take your uncle Kül as companion.
Heed my tongue when I offer counsel;
Thinking, ‘He will be a heavy mace,’
Keep me hanging at your belt.”
As Külchoro spoke thus,
The orphaned son of the hero
Revealed his valor;
As though stabbed in the heart,
He had gone away in wrath.
“True-born hero Seytek,
Braver than Semetey,
Has proved unworthy,” would they not say?
“The wretched orphan did not take after his father
And has come to nothing,” would they not say?
They would spread rumor and clamor,
Raising a great uproar that never fades.
“When driven into a trap, the stubborn one
Became as weak as straw,” would they not say?
“He lacked courage and did not take after his father;
He turned out worthless,” would they not say?
Like a hazy star in heaven,
He chose his appointed companion, would they not say?
“He means to attack the Chinese
And has taken as companion an uncle
Whose figure looms like a mountain,” would they not say?
Would not the people’s gossip devour him?
“He lost his nerve, unlike his father;
His life fled as though struck from above.
Unable to find the road through the dead end,
He wanders in confusion,” would they not say?
“Mighty Külchoro
Leads him by the hand,” would they not say?
Is there any yellow, hilly mountain
A hero cannot cross when he spurs on?
Wherever he went, your heroic father
Would take a companion.
Let me go with you as well.
Renowned Keң-Kol and great Talas—
Our forefather, brave Manas,
Found that land for us.
The fortunate Kyrgyz people there
Drank arak as though it were water.
It is the land my father proudly rode across,
The land where my mother bore me in labor,
The land where the blood was washed from my shirt,
The land where my umbilical cord was tied.
Broad Talas is where I wriggled
And crawled upon the dust,
Where I rode a switch naked
And played as a child.
Like the morning star Venus,
Let me go as your appointed companion;
My good fortune Seytek, let me
Go beside you as your companion.
Like white wheat flour,
Let me mingle closely with you;
Like the hair of a white gazelle,
Let me be drawn out beside you.
Knowing none can prevail against fate,
I give you this final counsel.
I speak it to you, my colt Seytek:
You need an elder brother.
My child, I need you to remain safe.
My child, many will narrow their eyes and mock you;
There are many wrathful enemies.
The Chinese stand along my flank;
Firearms face us ahead,
And many enemies oppose us.
What is needed against such foes?
To gird one’s loins, one needs a strong back.
One needs firm ground on which to stand,
Abundant courage and fierce might,
Power to straighten out whoever attacks,
And wisdom to ponder coming and going.
His bearing is rare, his spirit serene,
A fire that burns unlike any mortal.
His lashes are flame, his eyes are embers,
Among men there is no hero like him.
The companion who was speaking
Was utterly bewildered,
When the falcon surpassing all men
Set his face toward Talas.
Your poor, fierce mother,
The swift mare that seemed to fly,
The finest among all women,
The noble-born Aichürök,
Stately and majestic,
Fair-faced, with flashing eyes,
